doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: University in Toronto, learning percussion, return to Trinidad
summary: At York University he began serious percussion study, returned to Trinidad as a marine biologist and first-call percussionist, then moved to New York.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: constant struggle between the sciences and the arts. The sciences and the arts. When I went to university, and I went to university to study biogeography because I wanted to do forestry and ecology and stuff. At York University there was a Caribbean performing group on the campus. And I figured since nobody here knew me I would try and, you know, see if I could get back to a little bit of dance. And it so happened that the guy who was leading that knew of my performances in Trinidad because he had seen me perform with one of the biggest dance companies and all that type of stuff, knew that I was close to the drum. And a buddy of mine who was there encouraged me to start playing percussion. I used to play guitar, I had played trumpet, I had done all kinds of other things. And this thing started to get me deeper into myself, the whole realm of percussion, being introduced to the congas, not from the folk drum perspective of what we do in Trinidad and everything, which is commonplace and sacred in its own right, but to actually dedicate some time while my head was in academic mode, to consciously undertake the study of percussion. Go to class and do orchestral percussion and read pieces by these contemporary composers for percussion and everything hand claps and you know, all that type of stuff and everything else. It made a world of a difference. And as I started going deeper and deeper I started finding myself more and more and more and more. And I was a lost Caribbean son in a sea of Toronto. And I had never experienced winter before. I had never been among so many people who did not look like me before. It was culture shock, it was everything, and I was really trying to find myself. And I think this really brought me around. And throughout the rest of my university life I continued playing music. When I returned to Trinidad and I started working as a marine biologist, a marine research biologist, I had the opportunity to continue to play music because I was one of the — probably one of the few percussionists or may be the first even, to return to Trinidad having studied outside and having had the influence of the breadth of jazz and playing out and you know, working as a percussionist with stuff hanging all over you and having had the experience to see guys like Don and, you know, to study with Emile Latimer and everything else. When I got back to Trinidad I was one of the first call percussionists for visiting bands that was coming in, and I hooked up with some of the top players in Trinidad, guys like Len Boogsle Sharpe and Raf Robertson Clive Zanda — all those guys come from the calypso jazz tradition. And I just plugged right in. When I left and I came here, came out to live in New York, all I wanted to do was to play music. I didn’t want to do anything else. But I didn’t have any means to make a living you know. Because in Trinidad you know, your entire support system is there, you might be a big fish in a little pond. You get to New York and there are guys going [scats] all around you, you know what I mean? So I had to go back to study.
